title: What is prompt literacy? An exploratory study of language learners’ development of new literacy skill using generative AI
extended_summary:
This exploratory study asks whether a new form of literacy—“prompt literacy”—emerges when language learners use generative AI to complete a vocabulary-image creation task. The authors define prompt literacy as the ability to craft precise prompts, interpret generative-AI outputs, and iteratively revise prompts to achieve desired results.

The intervention was an AI-powered image creation project in which 30 EFL undergraduate students majoring in English Language and Literature used ChatGPT for vocabulary exploration and Bing Image Creator for generating images tied to the sociocultural or historical meanings of English words. Students read about word origins, researched further, sketched images, wrote prompts, revised them repeatedly, and compared generated images across iterations. Data sources included the generated artwork, a post-project survey adapted from a vocabulary learning questionnaire, and students’ reflection papers.

Findings show that students used repeated prompt revision to better specify context, character actions, and other details needed to generate intended images. Survey responses suggested high self-perceived gains in vocabulary-learning strategies such as visualization, attention to word origins, hidden meanings, and use in context. Reflections indicated that students viewed prompt literacy as enjoyable, useful for communication and problem-solving, and relevant to future human-AI collaboration. The paper argues that prompt literacy is an emerging AI-era literacy that can support vocabulary learning and creative language tasks, but it is an exploratory study rather than a controlled efficacy test.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot/LLM system used for conversational text generation, question answering, and assistance with drafting prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by EFL students to confirm word meanings, research additional information, and iteratively refine prompts for AI-generated images in a vocabulary-image creation project.

findings.finding_summary: The study reports qualitative evidence that students used ChatGPT iteratively to refine prompts and understand vocabulary origins and contexts, but it does not report a controlled comparison or outcome data isolating ChatGPT effects. The paper notes perceived improvement in vocabulary learning strategies after the project (n=30), but no tool-specific effect sizes or subgroup analyses are provided.
findings.measure: Self-perceived vocabulary learning strategies; reflection-based prompt literacy development

identified_tools.name: Bing Image Creator
identified_tools.description: Microsoft's text-to-image generative AI system for creating images from natural-language prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate and revise images representing the socio-cultural meanings and historical origins of English vocabulary items through iterative prompt refinement.

findings.finding_summary: Participants demonstrated prompt literacy by repeatedly revising prompts to better match intended images, indicating development of the ability to generate, interpret, and refine prompts for generative AI. The paper reports no experimental comparison group, no subgroup moderation, and no direct literacy test scores beyond self-reports and qualitative analysis.
findings.measure: Prompt revision behavior; qualitative analysis of generated images and reflections

quality_tier_rationale: This is a small qualitative/mixed-methods exploratory study with descriptive survey data and no true comparison group or causal estimate. It provides useful evidence about how students used generative AI in a literacy task, but not high-causal-credibility subgroup or differential-effects evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive but unquantified development of prompt literacy and self-perceived vocabulary strategy use, with no effect sizes. Any impact appears educationally meaningful but is not measured in a way that supports medium-or-large impact classification.
